samples.text: Mr. Secretary-General, The more I reflect on the theme of this session of the General Assembly, "Restoring trust and managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all," the more convinced I become of the wisdom of that choice. Without mutual trust, peace and security cannot take root among States. nor can cooperation among them flourish. More than 80 years ago, the United Nations was founded on the promise that the force of law would replace the law of force. Yet, we still live in a world of multiplying wars and conflicts, a world that spends more on armaments than on development. Civilians remain the primary victims. while millions face displacement, hunger, and deprivation. The problem is not the absence of rules. It is their selective application, if not their outright non-application. The sovereignty of states cannot be untouchable in one place and negotiable in another, nor can the rules of international law apply to some but not to others. Restoring trust requires respect for international law. It requires investment in preventing conflicts before they erupt and in development before poverty and deprivation become a source of violence, extremism, and terrorism. Development, too, is a matter of peace. There can be no sustainable peace in a world of widening economic disparities. where some states spend more on servicing their debt than on the health of their citizens and the education of their children. This does not absolve developing countries of the responsibility to undertake reform, combat corruption and build institutions. But those efforts require a fairer and more equitable international economic order, one that offers them genuine opportunities to advance. Mr. President, our shared responsibility is equally evident in the face of the profound transformations our world is undergoing. Climate change threatens the lives and livelihoods of millions. Those countries that have contributed least to it bear its gravest consequences. This calls for equitable adaptation, finance, and technology transfer. At the same time, the artificial intelligence revolution is opening unprecedented horizons for progress across every sphere of life.

Mr. President, Excellencies, as the UN Secretary General reminded us a few years ago, the United Nations is a product of hope. 81 years after its birth, that hope is being tested. Technology, including artificial intelligence, is advancing at rapid speed. Climate change is reshaping our societies. The international landscape is becoming more complex, more contested, and more unpredictable. The international order is not simply changing. It is being tested in an unprecedented manner. But it is in such times of uncertainty that the foundational values of multilateralism must be protected. International law, the UN Charter, respect for sovereign and territorial integrity, the peaceful settlement of disputes, respect for human rights, the quality of states, all these are not principles of the past. They are principles that transcend time, the essential ingredient for the present and for the future. The challenge before us is therefore clear. As the world changes, our institutions must be able to respond to new realities and threats while guided by the painful lessons of history and the vision of the founding fathers of this organization. And this is the essence of the theme of the 81st General Assembly, restoring trust, managing transformation, a United Nation that delivers for all. Ladies and gentlemen, transformation is inevitable. What must remain constant is the UN Charter as our compass. It directs all of us, irrespective of power, size, and leverage. For small-sized countries, the principle of equality of states is fundamental, and it has formed the binding trust between us. We rely on an international system in which sovereignty and territorial integrity are respected. We expect international law, including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, to be applied consistently. We believe in the peaceful resolution of disputes, and we demand that the rights of every state be protected. These are the integral elements of our collective trust And this is the code of conduct of Cyprus's diplomatic engagement. And in a rapidly changing world, small size states must seek synergies while continuing to pursue strategic autonomy.

Mr. President, Excellencies, my friends, we meet at a time when the obstacles confronting human progress are multiplying. Obstacles to peace, obstacles to food and clean water, obstacles to finance, medicine, and education, obstacles to movement and opportunity, obstacles to technology, to the knowledge and infrastructure needed to use it. And increasingly, obstacles between nations, between communities, and between people who no longer agree on the same facts or trust the same institutions. War continues to destroy lives and communities even though the international community possesses more tools than ever. Ever before to prevent conflict and to facilitate dialogue. The climate crisis is accelerating. Even though the science is clear enough for us to act, and many of the solutions are already known. And despite unprecedented global wealth, millions remain without reliable access to food, water, health, or shelter. These challenges, my friends, are creating the polycrises of which we constantly speak. And at the same time, new challenges are emerging. Artificial intelligence is opening extraordinary possibilities in health, education, science, and productivity, while also creating new risk of exclusion, exploitation, surveillance, and the distortion of truth. And yet the cooperation needed to confront these challenges is under strain. It is why I believe the theme this year is so apt, restoring trust. Managing transformation, a United Nation that delivers for all. The theme reminds us that we have institutions created to preserve peace, to advance development, and yes, to protect human dignity. The institutions are these very United Nations. We have shared principles grounded in sovereign equality and in the recognition that our responsibilities extend beyond borders. The Reality is that we understand that there is regrettably enough for us to be able to invest in prevention rather than waiting to finance reconstruction. We understand enough about the climate crisis to reduce the emissions that are warming our planet and take the necessary steps for our populations to adapt.

President of the General Assembly, United Nations Secretary-General, Heads of State and Government, Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Switzerland is a country of mountains, valleys and different languages. Part of our history, therefore, meant learning to live with what divides us. We didn't make the mountains disappear. First, we learned to climb them, then to cross them. To do so, we built roads, bridges and tunnels. And we realized that a natural boundary is not necessarily a dividing line. It can also be a pathway that connects us. This very simple experience seems to me to have something to teach us about the world in which we live. because we are going through a time of upheaval. The international order established in the aftermath of the Second World War is under severe constraints. Conflicts are multiplying and becoming deadlocked. The most fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter, the prohibition of the use of force and respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, are being openly violated. Added to this are transformations that are reshaping our societies. climate change and the increase in the number of disasters, humanitarian crises, inequalities, and also technological upheavals, notably artificial intelligence, which are often advancing faster than our collective ability to assess their implications. At the same time, multilateral institutions are having to respond to an increasing number of crises while facing pressure on resources and an erosion of trust. The theme of this 81st session of the General Assembly, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a United Nations that Delivers for All, therefore aptly sums up the task before us. To restore trust, to support transformation, and to demonstrate through concrete results that cooperation remains possible. This erosion of trust extends far beyond the realms of peace and security. We're also seeing it in the global economy. Protectionism is on the rise. Supply chains built up over decades of interdependence are being reorganized or fragmented as a result of geopolitical tensions. The multilateral trading system has been weakened. and the WTO can no longer fully carry out some of its essential functions.

Mr. President, Your Excellencies, we stand at the brink of a precipice. International law, as we know it, is challenged in an unprecedented manner. 80 years since the United Nations emerged out of World War II. Today, we stand before drastic, unpredictable geopolitical shifts, instability that appears to spiral, and an uncharted landscape that seems resistant to the international order and norms as we know them. We are witnessing devastating wars, and unimaginable humanitarian catastrophe and human suffering, blatant violations of international law and international humanitarian law that bring our system to its knees. We stand before the rise of use of force against sovereign states that constantly escalate and expand, threatening regional security and stability. States are sponsoring Malayan actors to destabilize, disrupting critical maritime routes. The use of new means of warfare is rising without even the most basic safeguards in place. Global security is constantly undermined. At the same time, We are faced with the challenge of the uncontrolled expansion of technology and AI threatening our security and the well-being of our children. And climate change is looming, threatening livelihoods, economies, creating new migration routes, and inequalities are becoming embedded. Our world is changing rapidly. And while there can be no doubt that the United Nations has served a noble cause and that together we have achieved tremendous progress, at this critical moment of inflection, we have a responsibility to recognize the shortcomings, to admit that we have lagged behind, that we have failed along the way, and these admissions need to steer us into action. We must urgently evolve to be fit to effectively address the immense, complex challenges we are faced with. Ladies and gentlemen, this is our moment of responsibility. Collective responsibility and individual state responsibility inextricably linked and mutually reinforcing. The scale and nature of the challenges we face require both. Better together is the theme of this year's assembly, but beyond better, we are also stronger together, more resilient together. This is a moment to renew our collective commitment and stand firmly and boldly in support of multilateralism and international law.
